analysis.one_liner: Bans health plans from imposing annual or lifetime dollar caps on benefits.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced in May 2009 with zero cosponsors, was referred to the Senate health committee and never received a markup or floor vote before that Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal health and employee-benefits law to prohibit group health plans, health insurers, and individual-market insurance from putting a total dollar cap on how much they will pay for a person's care in a year or over a lifetime. Under the bill, someone facing cancer or another catastrophic illness could not be cut off once their care hit a preset dollar amount. It would have taken effect for plan years starting one year after enactment. It was introduced in the Senate, sent to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients with catastrophic, expensive illnesses — cancer treatment, organ transplants, premature babies in intensive care, chronic conditions — who today can exhaust an annual or lifetime dollar cap and then must pay out of pocket or go without care. Family members who would otherwise be drained financially by a single serious illness also benefit, since the plan would have to keep paying once a cap is hit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seriously ill patients facing benefit caps

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits group health plans and health insurers from imposing an aggregate dollar annual or lifetime limit on benefits payable under a plan [S2][S3].
The ban is extended to health insurance sold in the individual market, applying the same protections to people who buy coverage on their own [S2][S3].

Under the bill's text, insurers could not cut off an individual's benefits once a preset dollar total was reached in a year or over a lifetime; the definition covers 'a dollar limitation on the total amount that may be paid with respect to such benefits' [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and employers that sponsor group plans would bear the cost of unlimited benefit liability. Insurers would likely raise premiums to cover the removed cap, spreading part of the cost across all policyholders, and employers sponsoring plans would pay more in contributions. The burden is concentrated on the small share of patients with extremely expensive care — and those are precisely the people the cap abandons.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employers with group plans

drawbacks.text: Without dollar caps, insurers and plan sponsors face unlimited liability for any single patient's care, and the honest cost of that shows up as higher premiums for everyone covered by a plan, not just the catastrophically ill [S3].

Higher premiums per covered worker could push some employers — especially small employers with thin margins — toward dropping coverage or shifting more costs to workers, so some of the bill's protection could be offset by coverage losses.

The bill is narrow: it removes dollar limits but does nothing else about insurance denials, exclusions for pre-existing conditions, or prices, so a patient could still be denied a specific treatment even if no dollar cap applies.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real and worth stating plainly: removing lifetime caps protects a small group of people from financial ruin from catastrophic illness, and pays for it in higher premiums spread across everyone in a plan. That is how insurance is supposed to work — the many pool against the rare catastrophe — and most people buying coverage accept that exchange. The bill's weakness is that it is a single provision; by itself it does not stop insurers from denying claims or excluding conditions, so its protection would be incomplete outside a broader law. The main practical objection is cost and premium pressure on plans and employers, not the principle.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee in May 2009, and the committee never took it up before that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced in the Senate on May 21, 2009, with Senator Reid introducing it on behalf of Senator Rockefeller, then read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S3][S5].
The action history ends with the referral; there was no committee markup, no floor debate, and no vote at any point [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2011, with the bill never reported out of committee [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the narrowest sense, insurers and plan sponsors avoided the cost of unlimited benefit liability under this particular bill. But the protection was not lost: Congress enacted the same ban on lifetime dollar limits — with restrictions on annual limits — in the Affordable Care Act in 2010, so patients gained the safeguard roughly a year after this bill stalled, through a broader law rather than this one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers, though the ACA soon delivered the same ban

for.name: Sen. John D. Rockefeller IV
for.role: U.S. Senator from West Virginia; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it to eliminate annual and lifetime dollar limits on health plan benefits.

for.name: Sen. Harry Reid
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on the sponsor's behalf on the Senate floor.

against.name: HELP Committee leadership
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or sent it to the floor; the bill stayed at referral for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor, no cosponsors, and no recorded votes, so the record shows no partisan pattern in support or opposition.

industries.note: The bill removes insurers' ability to cap their total payout on any one person, making them fully liable for catastrophic claims and likely raising premiums across the pool. Insurers' interest in keeping dollar caps runs against patients whose care exceeds them. Congress imposed the same ban in the ACA in 2010, so insurers faced the requirement anyway a year later.

Employers with group plans would face higher contributions as the bill eliminated dollar caps on their plans' liability. The cost is real but is the price of coverage no longer abandoning the most expensive patients.
